title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
raw_text: One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom. xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles . But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common. As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025. It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come. title: IFLA President’s Message October 2026
raw_text: This message was shared directly with all IFLA members and volunteers in all IFLA langauges earlier this month. Dear all, Another month has passed, and so time for another message sharing an update about what’s been going on at IFLA, and some of the key themes and questions on the agenda. It seems that every time I send one of these, I am arriving home from a period of travel. This time is no different – my latest engagement on behalf of IFLA was a great set of events first in Oslo at the National Library Forum hosted by the National Library of Norway where I had the opportunity to meet Åsa Wetås, the recently appointed Director of the National Library and then in South Africa, centred on the 17 th Stellenbosch University Library Symposium. The Symposium in Stellenbosch was particularly significant, marking the retirement of a great past IFLA President, Ellen Tise. I was also privileged to join an event organised by our Regional Office team at the University of South Africa. It’s been very welcome to see, across these events, how much the global field has embraced IFLA100 – our centenary – as an opportunity to take a moment for celebration and reflection. This is both about looking back and forwards. It was an honour not just to join Ellen, but also Kay Raseroka and Claudia Lux – two very distinguished past holders of my role! – and to share ideas about the trends that are shaping our field and Federation. title: Futures Club #6: You Can’t Create What You Can’t Imagine
raw_text: How can libraries help people think about the future? One of the clearest lessons from Futures Club #6, with Thomas Sture Rasmussen and Lotte Hviid Dhyrbye from the Danish Library Association was was that the answer is not to predict what will happen. Instead, libraries can give people the tools, spaces and confidence to explore different possible futures for themselves. The Association’s work was built on a combination of practical experience, as well as the record of the Library of the Future think-tank. The think tank had started as a form of aggregator, bringing together data and thinkers to prepare reports setting out visions of the future of libraries. However, over time, the emphasis shifted towards how to equip libraries to ask their own questions and imagine their own possibilities. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) had been particularly useful in this process. They provide both inspiration and a framework for conversations about the future we want. This can help overcome apathy, but also polarisation: instead of beginning with entrenched positions, people can start by discussing possibilities and shared aspirations. The SDGs have also helped libraries open conversations with organisations and sectors beyond the library field. The next step was to ask whether libraries could become futures literacy labs for their communities . title: A chance for a comprehensive approach? Knowledge and information in the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews
raw_text: Governments are recognising the role of knowledge and information in achieving progress across the United Nations’ 2030 Agenda, both as goals in themselves and as an enabler. They also underline the need for specialists, infrastructures, and intermediation. Yet a scattered way of doing things risks missing out on opportunities for a more strategic appraoch, notably one that realises the potential of libraries. IFLA has released its analysis of the 2026 Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs) of implementation of the SDGs, from the perspective of the contribution made by knowledge and information. The wealth of references to this serve as a strong indicator of both the strength and richness of this role. While there is unevenness in the number and variety of references from one Review to the next, these are present in every single review. As a result, both individually and collectively, the data points to a strong recognition of the different dimensions of the role of knowledge and information in sustainable development – as goals in their own right, and as an enabler of other goals. Some countries do look to measure these, but only in relatively narrow ways. There is also evidence of reflection on the need to uphold information integrity becoming part of wider sustainable development agendas. title: Finding My Place in the Global Library Community: Reflections from WLIC 2026
raw_text: Before attending WLIC 2026 in Busan , I knew IFLA through its sections, publications and meetings. Working in the Department of Foreign Relations at Türkiye’s Directorate General for Libraries and Publications, international cooperation was already part of my professional life. WLIC allowed me to experience the people behind that work. Being among more than 3,000 participants from over 100 countries and regions showed me that international librarianship depends as much on listening and understanding as on exchanging knowledge. For me, this connected closely to cultural diplomacy: cooperation often begins by understanding how others work, what they value and the challenges they face. As a Discovery Grant recipient, I attended business meetings on public libraries, national libraries, library design and literacy. I was interested in seeing how IFLA works from within: how priorities are discussed, different views are considered and members turn experience into collective work. Informal conversations were equally valuable, revealing perspectives that do not always emerge in formal sessions. Presenting my poster, “ Healing Library: A Public Library Perspective from Türkiye ,” let me share our experience while reconsidering it through colleagues’ questions. Rami Library’s IFLA Green Library Award was another proud moment, reminding me that experiences from Türkiye can contribute to wider professional discussions. title: Ladybird's first alpha release
raw_text: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. title: What happened at COP31, and what does it mean for the library field?
raw_text: In short: Despite COP31 ending without key cover agreements, actors from the culture sector made strong cases for our role in climate empowerment, adaptation, and resilience. Parties were unable to come to an agreement on the next Action for Climate Empowerment (ACE) action plan, although drafts had promising inclusion of information integrity and culture sector actors. IFLA’s volunteers, members, and partners had a record-breaking year for showcasing libraries of all kinds as drivers of climate action. Libraries showed real leadership in the culture sector, including through securing endorsements of heritage-based climate adaptation, the first Climate Library at a COP, and library commitments in the Heritage Adapts! initiative. We need community actors for climate now more than ever At the UN Climate Change Conference (COP), decisions require a compromise between national governments – including on a cover agreement. This is the conference’s key declaration of commitments countries will take on climate change. Consensus was not reaches due to the removal of fossil fuels from the draft declaration, which some States felt was unacceptable. While other decisions were made, the inability to agree on a core political outcome is widely considered a disappointment. Now more than ever, the role of communities, cities and local governments, civil society groups and institutions like libraries is needed to help people feel connected and empowered to make positive change. title: Management consulting is not a thin wrapper on intelligence
raw_text: By Rod Moshtagi and Sayash Kapoor. Moshtagi is a researcher at the Harvard Kennedy School and was previously a senior associate at PwC. In summer 2026, he was a GovAI fellow advised by Kapoor, and the research for this essay began as part of the fellowship. Many discussions of AI’s economic impact rest on the implicit assumption that most knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain. Management consulting is a compelling example. The visible outputs of consultants, such as research summaries, slide decks, and financial models, primarily comprise processing information , work that AI already excels at. If the main function of a consulting firm is to provide information, AI looks like an existential threat. Many commentators have drawn this conclusion. In 2025, The Free Press warned that “ the consulting crash is coming .” An analyst told Axios that consulting firms are “ going to run out of work .” In February 2026, the CEO of the AI startup Mercor predicted that “in the coming two years, we’re going to have chatbots that are as good as the best consulting firm.” In this essay, we argue that apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand both the value of consulting firms and how new technologies change the demand for consulting. title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
raw_text: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious). The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei – especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei. What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
raw_text: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. title: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
raw_text: On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug. The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise. The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week. raw_text: Hoe kan AI bijdragen aan een toekomstbestendig energiesysteem? title: Is het nieuws? – Wanneer je wel en geen persberichten stuurt
raw_text: Herkenbaar? Een collega vraagt of je snel een persbericht wilt versturen om aandacht te genereren voor een activiteit. Vaak zeggen we daar zonder aarzelen ‘ja’ op, maar de vraag is: heeft het onderwerp eigenlijk voldoende nieuwswaarde voor de media? In dit artikel helpen we je die afweging te maken met 4 praktische vragen. Daarnaast verkennen we alternatieven voor het persbericht, zodat je samen met collega’s kunt bepalen of er ook andere manieren zijn om mensen naar activiteiten te trekken? Lokale, regionale en landelijke redacties krijgen dagelijks tientallen persberichten binnen. In korte tijd beoordelen journalisten of een persbericht de moeite waard is om iets mee te doen of niet. Sylvia van Aartsen ( 2020 ), hoofd Kennis, Onderzoek & Communicatie van Cultuur Concreet, schrijft hierover: “Vaak kijken journalisten in eerste instantie niet verder dan de onderwerpregel en eventueel de eerste regels in het mailprogramma.” Kortom: geweldig dat er zondag over twee weken een lezing is met een lokale erfgoedspreker, maar die informatie is voor veel nieuwsredacties niet nieuwswaardig. Is het nieuws? Er is een aantal vragen die je kunt stellen, om te checken of er wel nieuwswaarde zit in wat je collega graag in de media terug zou zien. De belangrijkste is: wat maakt de gebeurtenis in jouw bibliotheek – jouw nieuwe programma, je nieuwe vestiging, je activiteiten tijdens de Kinderboekenweek – extra boeiend voor nieuwsredacties? title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
raw_text: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . title: Een kleine brand, grote gevolgen: wat de Bibliotheek Schiedam leerde over crisiscommunicatie
raw_text: Een brand in de Bibliotheek Schiedam zorgde afgelopen zomer voor een onverwachte sluiting en een omvangrijke schoonmaakoperatie. Naast alle praktische uitdagingen moest de bibliotheek de bezoekers, medewerkers en media informeren. Wat vraagt zo’n situatie van de communicatieafdeling? En welke lessen kunnen andere bibliotheekmarketeers hieruit trekken? Ook sprak ik met Suzanne Merema, Communicatie & PR-specialist bij Bibliotheek Schiedam. Op zondag 12 juli 2026 brak brand uit in de Korenbeurs, de centrale vestiging van de Bibliotheek Schiedam. Rond het middaguur ging het brandalarm af. Medewerkers schakelden de hulpdiensten in en brachten de bezoekers in veiligheid. Niemand raakte gewond en de brandweer had het vuur snel onder controle. Toch bleken de gevolgen aanzienlijk. Hoewel de brand beperkt bleef tot de omgeving van de toiletten, verspreidden rook en roet zich door het gebouw. Ook de boekencollectie werd getroffen. Uiteindelijk moesten duizenden boeken stuk voor stuk worden gereinigd. De bibliotheek moest tijdelijk sluiten. Daarmee ontstond niet alleen een grote operationele uitdaging, maar ook een communicatievraagstuk. Hoe informeer je bezoekers en medewerkers als nog niet duidelijk is hoelang de sluiting gaat duren? Wie staat de pers te woord? En hoe zorg je dat iedereen over dezelfde informatie beschikt? title: Het juiste verhaal op het juiste moment: profilering van de bibliotheek
raw_text: Voor veel bibliotheken is woordvoering niet iets van alledag. Een persvraag kan daardoor spannend voelen. Wie reageert er? En hoe zorg je dat diegene het juiste verhaal vertelt? Toch draait profilering om meer dan alleen het beantwoorden van vragen van journalisten. In elk moment dat de aandacht op de bibliotheek gericht is, ligt een kans om zichtbaar te maken waar je als organisatie voor staat. Onder andere via activiteiten, campagnes, samenwerkingen en persberichten laat je zien wat jouw bibliotheek betekent voor de omgeving. Woordvoering is hierin een belangrijk instrument. Meer dan een antwoord geven Elke bibliotheek heeft een sterk en eigen maatschappelijk verhaal. title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
raw_text: Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland. The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press . Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury , and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara . Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.
